meta.title: What fits in the file? — COF compared with character and memory formats
meta.description: Feature by feature: Character Open File (COF) compared with Character Card V2, Character Card V3 / .charx, agent Markdown (SOUL.md), Letta Agent File, MacPaw Portable Memory and VRM 1.0 — what each format carries, what it drops, and what COF does not try to do.
meta.og_title: What fits in the file? COF compared
meta.og_description: One table: personality, looks, voice, 3D, memories, psyche, rights and safety across seven formats AI characters travel in.

hero.sub: An AI character travels in many files — a card, a Markdown soul, an avatar, a memory bundle. One table of what each of them carries, and what it drops on the way.

lede: Nobody chose this. Role-play apps settled on the character card; agent frameworks on Markdown files; VTubers on VRM; memory projects on their own bundles. Each format is good at its layer and blind to the others, so a character that lives in several places exists as several files that drift apart. COF is the container that holds them together — a ZIP with a manifest, open, with rules about ages, rights and consent. This page compares it with the formats it embraces, feature by feature, including the ones COF does not have.
intro: Seven formats, as published: Character Card V2 (the chara PNG and its JSON, the de-facto standard of SillyTavern and its kin), Character Card V3 / .charx (its 2024 successor, a ZIP with assets), agent Markdown (SOUL.md, IDENTITY.md, AGENTS.md as OpenClaw and Hermes read them), Letta Agent File .af (a serialized stateful agent), MacPaw Portable Memory .mem (a user-owned memory bundle, 2026) and VRM 1.0 (the humanoid avatar on glTF, with the only mature permission block). Read as columns: what a file in that format can say about a character on its own, without the application that made it.

legend.y: native: the format has a field or a rule for it
legend.p: partly: text only, an opaque file, or a convention without a schema
legend.c: carried: COF keeps the other format's file inside, unchanged

h_not: What COF does not try to do

cards_not.p: A card is a picture you can post anywhere, and it stays a picture. A .cof is an archive. It exports a ccv3 PNG (and soon a .charx), but the file itself needs a tool that opens ZIPs — every tool does.

Letta's .af ships the tools, the tool rules, the model configuration and the message history. COF ships the character and declares executableContent: none. What runs it is the host's business, on purpose.
VRM defines the bones and the expressions. COF carries a VRM or a GLB as a file, with its rights and its textures, and adds the poses, the clips and the voice around it. The rig stays VRM's.
MacPaw's .mem writes tombstones and an audit log, so a forgotten memory can be shown to have been forgotten everywhere. COF purges on export (cof extract) and keeps no trace of it — yet.

cards_only.p: One file, several ready-to-use combinations: the same character at 29 and at 65, for work and for everyone, in French and in Japanese. Other formats need one file per version, and the versions drift.

cards_only.t: A past and an inner life, with a why
cards_only.p: Dated memories with who, where, what and how it felt; a psyche of values, beliefs, wants and fears, each tied to the memory it comes from, with a strength and a time span. Agent formats keep prose; memory formats keep events; neither keeps the link between the two.

Every preset declares an age; nudity or intimate content with a minor makes the file invalid, not merely tagged. A real person needs a consent record. Executables, pickles and unsafe paths are refused. Nobody has to trust the author's good faith.
What the character lived in OpenClaw, in Hermes or in a chat comes back into the same file as new, personal memories (cof memory add) — and leaves with the user. One character, two homes, one memory.

embrace1: The point of the table is not that COF wins the most ticks. It is that COF does not ask anyone to abandon anything: a .cof contains a valid Character Card V3, exports a ccv3 PNG, a card JSON, SOUL.md / IDENTITY.md and a whole agent workspace, and keeps a VRM as a plain file. The formats in the other columns are its inputs and its outputs. Where COF has no equivalent — a rig, a runtime, a signed deletion — the right move is to carry the other format, and the table says so with a ${CARRIED}.
embrace2: The grey rows are promises with a date, not features. They come from the public roadmap; the RFCs that change the format are open for comments before they ship.
sources: Character Card V2 — the chara_card_v2 specification (SillyTavern, Risu, Chub) and its PNG tEXt chara embedding.
Character Card V3 / CHARX — kwaroran/character-card-spec-v3, SPEC_V3.md (MIT): assets, creator_notes_multilingual, source[], dates, group_only_greetings, the embeded://assets/ folders.
Agent Markdown — OpenClaw's SOUL.md / IDENTITY.md, Hermes Agent profiles, the AGENTS.md convention; what COF writes is documented in the 1.2.2 notes.

Letta Agent File — letta-ai/agent-file (Apache-2.0) and the AgentFileSchema of the letta package: agents, groups, blocks, files, sources, tools, mcp_servers, skills; no passages, no format version field.
MacPaw Portable Memory — MacPaw/portable-memory (MIT), format 1.1: episodes, resources by reference, tombstones, CHECKSUMS, optional Ed25519 signatures; RFC 0001–0003 towards 1.2.

VRM 1.0 — vrm-c/vrm-specification: humanoid bones, 18 expression presets, the meta permission block (avatar permission, violent and sexual usage, commercial use, redistribution, modification, credit).
COF — spec 1.2, RFC 0002–0006, roadmap. Corrections welcome through the issues: a wrong mark in this table is a bug.
footer: Character Open File — an open format for AI characters, with their rights. Specification CC BY 4.0, tools MIT. Formats named here belong to their authors; this comparison reads their published specifications, as of November 2026. Source on GitHub · About the format
